why: Briefing is explicit that no harness delivers a notification off the machine. To do this today I would have to wire a Notification hook to ntfy/Pushover myself — a setup project, not 30 seconds, and the briefing says a normal user has not wired hooks. Impact is high because it is the difference between actually walking away and babysitting panes.

No harness distinguishes a wedged agent from a productive one — both keep emitting. Telling them apart by hand means watching one pane over minutes and judging whether the output is progress, which is correlation across time that nobody does reliably across 3-12 sessions. Getting it instantly stops real token and hour burn on loops.

Requires retained, queryable history of my own repeated interventions across sessions, which the briefing says no harness keeps. By hand it is pure memory — I would never notice the fifth repetition. But the outcome is an occasional automation win I can defer indefinitely, so it changes little day to day.

A subagent and its stage are printed in the session that spawned it, so looking at that pane gets me the stage; Spacedock stage state is also on disk. The tripwire half — alert me when a stage is reached — needs custom work. Mixed access. Value is real steering but only for the subset of sessions running staged workflows.

No harness retains queryable cross-session history, so streaks and weekly counts would mean grepping session files on disk and aggregating — reachable but nobody does it. The item itself says no decision attached, and I agree: I would look once, feel something, and change nothing.

In Claude Code I type /usage and get the weekly figure with its reset; a Barista-style status line puts it on screen unprompted. One command in a place I know. Knowing it changes what I schedule for the week and avoids hitting the weekly wall mid-task, but the decision comes up on a weekly rhythm, not hourly.

Claude exposes a Notification hook but the briefing says a normal user has not wired it, and it covers one harness. Without it my only method is cycling tabs to see what changed — the definition of unreliable correlation across sessions. Push instead of poll removes a constant background tax on attention.

git status is one command I know, but I have to remember which sessions ended and cd into each repo or worktree to run it — several places, manual work, and the ended sessions are exactly the ones I stop looking at. Impact is high because uncommitted work in an abandoned worktree is concrete lost work, not an inconvenience.

This needs every session state plus a forward estimate of when the next one will want me, and the briefing says no harness estimates turn duration at all. Nothing I can type gets it. Reliably knowing I have twenty clear minutes genuinely changes behaviour — I leave the desk instead of hovering — though it does not by itself prevent a loss.

Quota is shown as a current figure only; no harness projects it forward. I would have to note /usage twice, time the interval and do the arithmetic myself, per harness — reachable but not something I do reliably mid-work. Seeing the wall coming an hour out lets me resequence a long job instead of being cut off inside it.
